title: Version Control (Git)
description: Keeping a team repository safe: conflicts at scale, hooks, branch protection and signed commits.
resumo: `zdiff3` shows the ancestor; `rerere` replays known resolutions; in a rebase, ours/theirs are swapped.
Resolve conflicts file by file — never `checkout --theirs .` on everything.
Hooks (`core.hooksPath`) are fast local conveniences; CI runs the real checks.
Protect main: PRs, approvals, required checks, no force push — for admins too.
CODEOWNERS: the last matching pattern wins — general rules first.
Sign commits (SSH or GPG) and add the key to GitHub as a signing key.

subsections.subtitle: Advanced Conflict Resolution
subsections.description: Tools for complex and repeated conflicts.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a long-running branch is rebased every day, and the same conflict has to be resolved again each time.

**Concept:** conflicts shrink when you integrate often, keep commits small and update your branch with main regularly. The `zdiff3` conflict style also shows the common ancestor, so it is clear what each side changed. `git rerere` remembers how you resolved a conflict and reapplies it when the same conflict comes back. During a rebase, `--ours` and `--theirs` are swapped: "ours" is the branch you are rebasing onto, usually main.

**How it works:** after resolving, run the tests: a merge without textual conflicts can still break the logic.
examples.code:
git config --global merge.conflictstyle zdiff3
git config --global rerere.enabled true

git merge origin/main
git checkout --ours   path/file    # in a merge: keep your version (in a rebase, the opposite)
git checkout --theirs path/file    # in a merge: keep the incoming version
git add path/file && git commit
examples.interview_question: Which practices reduce and simplify merge conflicts?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Taking one side for every file to "finish quickly". `git checkout --theirs .` throws away all of your changes in conflicting files, not only the conflicting lines. Resolve file by file.
examples.code:
# WRONG: discards your side of every conflicting file
git checkout --theirs .
git add . && git commit

# RIGHT: look at each conflict
git status                        # list the conflicting files
git mergetool                     # or edit them one by one

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** commits with broken formatting and messages outside the convention keep reaching the pull request, and CI fails on trivial things.

**Concept:** hooks are scripts that Git runs on events: `pre-commit` (format and lint), `commit-msg` (validate the message format), `pre-push` (quick tests). They live in `.git/hooks` and are not versioned; to share them with the team, point `core.hooksPath` to a folder in the repository.

**How it works:** hooks are a convenience for developers; CI still runs the real checks, because a hook can always be skipped.
examples.code:
# .githooks/commit-msg
#!/bin/sh
if ! grep -qE '^(feat|fix|docs|refactor|test|chore|ci)(\(.+\))?!?: .+' "$1"; then
  echo "Commit message does not follow Conventional Commits"
  exit 1
fi

git config core.hooksPath .githooks
chmod +x .githooks/commit-msg
examples.interview_question: What are Git hooks used for?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A slow `pre-commit` that runs the whole test suite. Every commit takes minutes, so people start using `--no-verify` and the hook protects nothing. Keep hooks to a few seconds; leave the full suite to CI.
examples.code:
# WRONG: pre-commit
./mvnw verify          # 6 minutes per commit -> everyone runs git commit --no-verify

# RIGHT: pre-commit only formats and lints changed files; CI runs mvn verify

subsections.subtitle: Branch Protection and the PR Flow
subsections.formerSubtitle: Proteção de Branches e Fluxo de PR

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** someone pushes straight to main, or merges with CI red, and production breaks.

**Concept:** protection rules on main: no direct pushes and no force pushes; pull requests with at least one approval; required CI status checks (build and tests); the branch up to date before merging. A `CODEOWNERS` file names required reviewers per area of the code. Squash merging keeps one commit per PR on main, which makes reverts easy.

**How it works:** apply the rules to administrators too, so nobody bypasses them under pressure.
examples.interview_question: How do you protect the main branch in a team repository?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: A catch-all rule at the end of `CODEOWNERS`. The last matching pattern wins, so `*` at the bottom overrides every specific rule above it, and the payments team is never asked to review payment code. Put the general rule first.
examples.code:
# WRONG: "*" is last, so it wins for every file
/src/main/java/com/shop/payment/    @payments-team
*                                   @platform-team

# RIGHT: general first, specific after
*                                   @platform-team
/src/main/java/com/shop/payment/    @payments-team

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** anyone can set `user.name` and `user.email` to someone else's and commit as them.

**Concept:** a cryptographic signature (GPG or SSH) proves the commit was made by the owner of the key. GitHub shows a "Verified" badge and can require signed commits on protected branches — a supply-chain defense.

**How it works:** with SSH signing, the same kind of key you already use for push can sign commits.
examples.code:
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true

git log --show-signature -1

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Adding the SSH key to GitHub only as an authentication key. Push works, but commits show "Unverified", because GitHub only trusts keys added as signing keys. Add the same public key again with the type "Signing key".
examples.code:
# Commits show "Unverified" on GitHub

# RIGHT: GitHub → Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key
#        Key type: Signing Key   (in addition to the Authentication Key)
gh ssh-key add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub --type signing
